blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — safe specimen transport
stem: A facility permits a routine laboratory specimen to be sent through its validated pneumatic tube system. What should the nurse do before sending it?

options.A: Verify the specimen identity, secure the primary container closed, and use the facility-approved leak-resistant transport containment for the tube system.
options.B: Loosen the specimen cap before transport so pressure changes can vent through the opening while the carrier moves through the tube system.
options.C: Remove the specimen label after placing it in the carrier because the pneumatic carrier serves as the specimen identifier during transport.
options.D: Place the specimen directly in the carrier without secondary containment whenever the primary container appears intact before transport.

rationale: A is correct. OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard requires blood or other potentially infectious material specimens to be in containers that prevent leakage and to be closed before transport. If outside contamination occurs, a leak-preventing secondary container is required. CDC laboratory-safety guidance identifies leakage or breakage as a major pneumatic-tube hazard and supports facility-specific risk assessment and safe-handling procedures. B and D increase leakage risk, and C creates an identification error.
educational_objective: Before pneumatic-tube transport of an approved routine specimen, verify identification, secure closure, and facility-approved leak-resistant containment.
source_organization: U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA); Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC); NCSBN
source_document_title: 29 CFR 1910.1030 — Bloodborne pathogens; laboratory specimen-transport safety guidance; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan
source_version_date: Current OSHA regulation live-rechecked 2026-08-21; CDC pneumatic-tube/laboratory safety guidance currentness rechecked 2026-08-21; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan effective April 2026
source_locator: OSHA 1910.1030(d)(2)(xiii): specimens of blood/OPIM must be in a container preventing leakage during transport; 1910.1030(d)(2)(xiii)(A): transport container must be closed before transport; (B): if outside contamination occurs, place primary container in a second container that prevents leakage. CDC clinical-laboratory biosafety review, Specimen Transport/Pneumatic tube transport: tight-fitting lids, leak-resistant secondary containment, and leakage/breakage are central pneumatic-tube hazards.
source_claim_supported: Current OSHA requirements directly support closed, leak-preventing specimen containment during transport; CDC laboratory-safety evidence supports pneumatic-tube risk controls and facility-specific safe handling.
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control, printed p.8: handle biohazardous materials safely, identify clients correctly, and use equipment appropriately.
pdf_visual_verification: PASS — official 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan Safety and Infection Prevention and Control page was screenshot-verified earlier in this continuation; transport claims rely on current OSHA HTML and CDC laboratory-safety evidence.

option_audit.A: Correct; combines specimen identity, secure closure, and leak-resistant approved transport containment.
option_audit.B: Plausible pressure-management misconception but deliberately defeats the required closed leak-preventing container.
option_audit.C: Plausible carrier-tracking misconception but removing specimen identification creates a safety error.
option_audit.D: Plausible minimal-containment shortcut but ignores facility-approved containment and pneumatic leakage/breakage risk.

cueing_audit.answer_length: All options are similar in structure and detail; the key is not uniquely signaled by length.
cueing_audit.absolute_words: No distractor depends on simplistic always/never/only wording.
